Marles was asked about home affairs minister Tony Burke’s delayed speech before the National Press Club about migration policies.

The deputy prime minister said the decision was merely a move of date, not a cancellation. Marles said:

It’s not unusual for dates to be moved around in people’s diaries and in terms of presenting speeches of that kind. I think what’s important here in terms of migration policy is complex. It’s one that we’ve been working on since we’ve come to government.

Tony Burke will be talking about that and he’ll be talking about that at the National Press Club at the earliest opportunity.

Moving around dates in a diary for senior members of government is very routine. It happens literally all the time. The speech hasn’t been called off. A date has been changed. That literally happens every week. And there’s nothing more to it than that.

New Victoria premier pushes on with work-from-home laws

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, who took over as leader after an internal revolt against Jacinta Allan, will continue pursuing the laws she championed, AAP reports.

The legislation would give full-time, part-time and casual workers the right to work from home two days a week on a pro-rata basis where reasonable.

The bill has already passed the Labor-controlled lower house and will soon be debated in the upper house as the November state election approaches.

It has attracted staunch opposition from business lobby groups, which have met with Carroll since his elevation to premier. But a Victorian government spokesperson confirmed on Friday the government’s position had not changed.

Among the more contentious elements of the bill is a requirement for employers to pay any reasonable costs to allow an eligible employee to work remotely. This may include essential equipment and secure access to work systems.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has accused Pauline Hanson of betraying voters who donate to One Nation, after reports she used the party's funds to pay for a luxury London hotel during her recent trip to Europe.

Nine Newspapers report Hanson used the party's funds to pay for the stay at Conrad London St James hotel, where rooms cost an average of $860 per night in peak season, including for five days while she travelled to Italy on Gina Rinehart's dime.

One Nation insists the funds used were not part of the $5 million raised by the party's 'fire the liar' viral fundraising campaign.

Speaking to the Today Show, Wilson has accused Hanson of looking like a "global elite".

"We have people who donate to her party from their limited savings, they're struggling to get ahead and now we find it's going towards luxury hotel rooms in London."

"I'm starting to see images of global elite.

"This seems like a pretty clear betrayal of the people she claims to represent."

By Ewa Staszewska, Oliver Gordon and Clare Armstrong

Internal pressure is growing on the federal government to strengthen its gambling reforms, with more Labor MPs calling for an end to inducements used to entice people to keep wagering.

The draft legislation is friendless in its current form, with the Coalition, Greens and crossbenchers all calling for sweeping amendments to ensure children and vulnerable Australians are protected from gambling harm.

The government insists negotiations continue despite an ABC report that Labor would consider shelving the reforms rather than entertain major rewrites.

Calls for strong action on inducements follow explosive allegations that gambling company employees offered to secure drugs and escorts for those gambling, revealed during a two-day Senate inquiry earlier this week. Betting giants have denied the claims.
